Lesson 4 Overview

By the end of this lesson, you will have learned how the DREI framework uses <ai prompt="What is levelized cost of electricity?">levelized cost of electricity 💬️</ai> (LCOE) modelling to connect investment risk, financing costs, and renewable energy competitiveness.

You will understand how public instruments affect the weighted average cost of capital (WACC), and how these changes translate into lower LCOE values for renewable projects.
The lesson does not focus on detailed financial modelling techniques, which have already been introduced earlier in the Academy.

Instead, it emphasizes the role of LCOE within the DREI framework: providing a consistent, transparent metric to compare the impact of different derisking strategies across technologies and country contexts.
By working through this lesson, you will see how policymakers and stakeholders can use LCOE results to evaluate trade-offs, prioritize public interventions, and communicate the benefits of derisking in clear, quantifiable terms.
M5: Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI)
A: Calculating Life Cycle Costs and incremental costs of renewable energy investment
The modelling of the Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) helps to evaluate the cost competitiveness of the renewable energy technology under consideration.
LCOE represents the average cost of electricity generation over the lifetime of a project, incorporating investment, operation, maintenance, and financing costs.

It provides a clear, comparable metric for assessing the economic viability of different energy technologies.

The LCOE is calculated using the DREI LCOE Tool, which combines technical and financial inputs based on the national and technological context.
These include data on capital expenditure, operations and maintenance, system lifetime, generation performance, and financing conditions.

The tool uses the financing costs identified earlier in the process—both before and after the application of public derisking instruments.

Data collection for this modelling involves technical assumptions that can often be drawn from national energy planning or feasibility studies.
Financial parameters, particularly the cost of equity and debt, are based on investor input collected through structured interviews.
In some contexts, barriers to obtaining accurate data may include lack of transparency, limited availability of disaggregated cost figures, or uncertain pricing of fossil fuel alternatives.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
LCOE Modelling Lets You Compare Renewable and Fossil Costs

The LCOE modelling provides estimates of the Business as Usual electricity production costs (LCOE) for the Baseline technology (usually a fossil fuel based technology) and for the renewable energy technology considered in the study
Derisking Shows How Renewables Can Compete with Business-as-Usual
The impacts of the derisking instruments on the cost of capital are evaluated, and the resulting LCOE for the renewable energy technology after derisking is compared with the Business-as-Usual LCOEs.
